cues.text: The Eve of Corpus Christi

On June 2, 1649, in the small coastal town of Eten, in the province of Chiclayo in northern Peru, a Corpus Christi celebration was underway in the parish founded not long before by Spanish settlers among the local Mochica community.

As the priest prepared to return the monstrance to the tabernacle after the blessing of the Blessed Sacrament, several of the faithful present reported seeing something extraordinary appear on the consecrated Host itself.
The Face of a Child

Witnesses described the radiant face of an infant, with brown curling hair, appearing where the Host had been — an image vivid and clear enough that word of it spread quickly through the town and the surrounding region.
The event was not isolated: a second apparition followed weeks later, on July 22, the feast of St. Mary Magdalene.
The town’s own patron saint, it showed the Christ Child dressed in a purple tunic, in the traditional style worn by Eten’s people themselves.
A Local Devotion for Centuries
The images of the Divine Child of the Miracle became, and have remained, a defining devotion of Eten and its largely Indigenous Mochica community.
They have drawn pilgrims from across Peru for well over three centuries.
The devotion is commemorated with an annual feast running from July 12 to 24, including the ceremonial transfer of the miraculous Host between its sanctuary and the town church.
A Bishop's Advocacy
From 2015 to 2023, the cause for formal Vatican recognition of the Eten account gained unusual momentum under Robert Prevost, bishop of Chiclayo.
Chiclayo is the diocese that includes Eten.

Prevost personally celebrated Mass at the site, encouraged devotion to the Divine Child, and in 2019 delivered to Pope Francis a formal dossier documenting the tradition, including more than twenty thousand testimonies from the faithful.

Prevost was elected pope in 2025, taking the name Leo XIV, and residents of Eten have since renewed hope that formal recognition — which would make Eten the first officially recognized Eucharistic miracle site in the Americas — may follow.
Legacy
Unlike most accounts in this exhibition, the Eten tradition remains an open question rather than a settled one.
It has not yet received formal diocesan or papal recognition that would place it alongside Europe’s approved Eucharistic miracles.
Its cause continues through the Church's own deliberate process of investigation.
What is not in question is the devotion itself, which is nearly four centuries old.
An Indigenous community has carried it forward, keeping the Divine Child of the Miracle at the center of its religious life since long before any pope from its own region took interest in the case.
